facts: Southend Pier is the longest pleasure pier in the world, extending over 2 kilometres into the Thames Estuary.
A miniature railway has run along the pier since 1890.
The pier has survived several major fires over its history and remains a working attraction.
Colchester Castle has the largest surviving Norman keep in Europe, larger even than the White Tower of London.
It was built on the foundations of a Roman temple to the Emperor Claudius.
Colchester is recognised as Britain's oldest recorded town, referenced by Roman writers as Camulodunum.
King's College Chapel has the largest fan vault ceiling in the world, completed in 1515.
Its Nine Lessons and Carols service, broadcast every Christmas Eve, has been held since 1918.
Cambridge is one of the oldest universities in the world, founded in 1209.
Ely Cathedral is nicknamed the 'Ship of the Fens' for its dramatic visibility across the flat surrounding landscape.
Its unique octagonal lantern tower, built after the original tower collapsed in 1322, is a masterpiece of medieval engineering.
Ely was the last part of England to hold out against William the Conqueror, led by Hereward the Wake.
Norwich has more medieval churches surviving than any other city in Western Europe north of the Alps.
Norwich Cathedral's spire is the second-tallest in England, after Salisbury.
Norwich Castle's keep was built as a royal palace, one of the largest Norman keeps in England.
Bury St Edmunds Abbey was once one of the richest and most powerful monasteries in medieval England.
Barons are said to have sworn an oath here in 1214 that helped lead to Magna Carta.
The town takes its name from King Edmund, martyred by Vikings and buried at the abbey.
Newmarket is often called the headquarters of British horse racing, with roots dating to James I in the 1600s.
The National Horseracing Museum tells the story of the sport in the town.
Newmarket has more racehorses in training than any other town in Britain.
Painter Thomas Gainsborough was born in Sudbury in 1727; his family home is now a gallery.
Sudbury is the largest town on the River Stour in Suffolk.
The town is the terminus of a branch line from Marks Tey, sometimes called the 'Gainsborough Line'.
The Stour Valley around Manningtree inspired many of John Constable's most famous landscape paintings.
Manningtree claims to be England's smallest town by area.
Flatford Mill, painted in Constable's 'The Hay Wain', lies a short distance from the town.
Harwich has been a significant port since medieval times, later a base for the Royal Navy.
The Mayflower's captain, Christopher Jones, is believed to have lived in Harwich before the 1620 voyage.
Harwich International station connects directly to ferry services to the Hook of Holland.
Felixstowe is the busiest container port in the United Kingdom.
The town also developed as a genteel Victorian seaside resort alongside its port trade.
Felixstowe sits at the mouth of the Rivers Orwell and Deben.
Great Yarmouth's seafront 'Golden Mile' has been a traditional British seaside resort since Victorian times.
The town was once one of the largest herring fishing ports in the world.
Great Yarmouth's Row houses are a distinctive network of narrow medieval alleyways.
Cromer crab is a local delicacy, caught by small boats working directly off the beach.
Cromer Pier's Pavilion Theatre hosts one of the last traditional end-of-pier variety shows in Britain.
The town's church has the tallest tower in Norfolk.
The North Norfolk Railway, nicknamed the 'Poppy Line', runs a heritage steam service from Sheringham.
Sheringham Park, nearby, was landscaped by renowned designer Humphry Repton.
Sheringham remains a working fishing town alongside its tourism.
Stansted's terminal building was designed by architect Norman Foster, opened in 1991.
It is one of London's main airports, particularly for budget airlines.
The station sits directly beneath the terminal for a seamless rail connection.
Audley End House was once so vast that it was said to rival royal palaces in scale.
It was built in the early 17th century for Thomas Howard, Earl of Suffolk.
The surrounding parkland was landscaped by Capability Brown.
Cecil Rhodes, the controversial colonial figure, was born in Bishop's Stortford in 1853.
The town's castle, Waytemore Castle, has origins dating back to Norman times.
Bishop's Stortford sits on the River Stort, close to the Hertfordshire-Essex border.
Upminster Windmill, built in 1803, is one of the best-preserved smock mills in Essex.
Upminster sits at the eastern end of the District line as well as c2c services.
The area retains a village-like character despite being within Greater London.
Tilbury Fort is one of the finest examples of 17th-century military engineering in England.
Elizabeth I delivered her famous speech to troops nearby ahead of the Spanish Armada in 1588.
Tilbury Docks later became a major arrival point for immigration, including the Empire Windrush in 1948.
Frinton-on-Sea was developed from the 1890s as a deliberately quiet, upmarket alternative to nearby Clacton.
The town famously had no pubs for most of the 20th century.
Frinton's Greensward promenade remains a well-preserved Edwardian seafront.
Clacton Pier opened in 1871 and remains one of the most visited piers on the East Anglian coast.
Clacton was purpose-built as a seaside resort by Peter Bruff, who also built the railway to serve it.
The town continues to host traditional funfair rides and amusements.
The Naze cliffs are rich in fossils, eroding steadily into the North Sea.
A Napoleonic-era tower, the Naze Tower, stands as a landmark on the clifftop.
Walton-on-the-Naze developed as a resort after the railway arrived in 1867.
Liverpool Street is one of the busiest stations in Britain, serving both the City of London and Stansted Airport.
The adjoining Broadgate development was one of the first major office redevelopments of the 1980s.
A memorial at the station commemorates the Kindertransport, which brought thousands of refugee children to Britain.
Fenchurch Street is the only central London terminus with no direct London Underground connection.
It is the smallest of London's main railway termini.
The station is the London end of the c2c line to Southend and Shoeburyness.
The London Stadium, built for the 2012 Olympics, became West Ham United's home ground in 2016.
West Ham is a major interchange station serving multiple London Underground and Overground lines.
The surrounding Stratford area was extensively regenerated for the Olympic Games.
Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park was the main site for the London 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
The ArcelorMittal Orbit, in the park, is Britain's largest piece of public art.
Stratford station is one of the busiest interchanges in London.
Epping Forest is one of the largest surviving areas of ancient woodland near London.
It has been protected as public open space since the Epping Forest Act of 1878.
Waltham Cross sits close to the forest's western edge, at the boundary of Essex and Hertfordshire.
Waltham Abbey is said to be the burial place of King Harold, defeated at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.
The town's Eleanor Cross, one of the surviving monuments to Edward I's queen, still stands nearby.
Waltham Cross station serves the town on the West Anglia Main Line.
Hertford Castle's surviving gatehouse dates from the 15th century, built on earlier Norman foundations.
Hertford is the county town of Hertfordshire.
The town sits at the confluence of four rivers.
Hatfield Forest is considered one of the best-preserved medieval royal hunting forests in Europe.
It retains its historic combination of woodland, grassland and ancient pollarded trees.
The forest is managed by the National Trust.
Braintree was historically a centre of wool weaving and later silk manufacturing.
Courtaulds, a major British textile firm, had its origins in Braintree's silk mills.
The town sits at the meeting point of two Roman roads.
Chelmsford Cathedral became a cathedral only in 1914, though the church itself dates from the 15th century.
Chelmsford is recognised as the birthplace of radio broadcasting, home to Marconi's early wireless factory.
Chelmsford is the county town of Essex.
Southend Airport has a direct rail link into its terminal, opened in 2011.
The airport has one of the shortest security queues of London's airports due to its smaller scale.
It sits close to Rochford, a historic Essex market town.
Rochford's market square retains its medieval layout at the heart of the town.
The town sits on the River Roach, close to Southend Airport.
Rochford was historically the administrative centre for the wider Rochford Hundred area.
Basildon was designated one of Britain's post-war new towns in 1949.
The town absorbed several older plotland settlements built informally in the early 20th century.
Basildon has become a significant retail and commercial centre in south Essex.
Purfleet was once home to a Royal Gunpowder Magazine, supplying the British military for over a century.
The town sits on the north bank of the Thames Estuary.
Purfleet has seen significant riverside regeneration in recent years.
Grays developed around chalk quarrying and lime production on the Thames.
Important prehistoric elephant remains have been discovered in the town's former quarry pits.
Grays sits opposite Dartford across the Thames.
Barking Abbey was once one of the most important nunneries in medieval England.
Only fragments of the abbey, including the Curfew Tower gatehouse, survive today.
Barking sits on the River Roding in east London.
Ford's Dagenham plant opened in 1931 and was once the largest car factory in Europe.
The 1968 Ford sewing machinists' strike here helped lead to the Equal Pay Act.
Dagenham Dock station serves the industrial riverside area of the borough.
Wivenhoe sits on the River Colne, historically an important shipbuilding town.
The University of Essex campus lies a short distance from the town.
Wivenhoe's colourful waterside houses are a well-known local landmark.
Sutton Hoo, near Woodbridge, is the site of one of the most important Anglo-Saxon ship burial discoveries in Britain.
Woodbridge itself has a well-preserved tide mill dating back centuries.
The town sits on the River Deben in Suffolk.
Ipswich is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in England, with Anglo-Saxon origins.
Its regenerated waterfront now hosts university buildings and marina developments.
Ipswich was the birthplace of Cardinal Thomas Wolsey, chief advisor to Henry VIII.

landmark: Stowmarket's Museum of East Anglian Life
facts: The Museum of East Anglian Life preserves rural crafts, agriculture and industry from the region's past.
Stowmarket sits on the River Gipping in central Suffolk.
The town was historically a centre of malting and agricultural trade.
Diss Mere, a natural lake at the heart of the town, has been a feature since medieval times.
The town's timber-framed Dolphin House is one of its most photographed buildings.
Diss sits right on the Norfolk-Suffolk border.
Beccles sits on the River Waveney, a popular base for exploring the Norfolk and Suffolk Broads.
The town's detached bell tower, standing apart from its church, is a distinctive local landmark.
Beccles has a long tradition as a market and boating town.
Lowestoft Ness is the most easterly point of mainland Britain.
The town was once a major herring fishing port, alongside Great Yarmouth.
Lowestoft's lighthouse has guided ships since the 17th century.
Wymondham Abbey has two towers, reflecting a historic dispute between the monks and the townspeople over the building.
The town's name is traditionally pronounced 'Windham'.
Wymondham was the birthplace of Robert Kett, leader of a major 1549 rebellion.
Attleborough's parish church retains a rare surviving medieval rood screen.
The town has held a market since at least the 13th century.
Attleborough sits between Norwich and Thetford in south Norfolk.
Thetford Forest is the largest lowland pine forest in England, largely planted after the First World War.
The town was once one of the largest in England, with a former cathedral and royal palace.
Thetford was the birthplace of Thomas Paine, author of Common Sense and Rights of Man.

landmark: Wroxham, capital of the Norfolk Broads
facts: Wroxham is often called the unofficial capital of the Norfolk Broads, a network of navigable rivers and lakes.
The Broads were once thought natural but are now known to be flooded medieval peat diggings.
The village is a major hub for boat hire on the Broads.
